title: Unified SDK transport profiles: conservative/balanced/aggressive presets and stream-first retry ergonomics
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Create and ship a set of opinionated, documented transport presets for Python/TS/Go SDKs (conservative, balanced, aggressive) that cover connection pooling, keep-alive, per-route latency windows, and retry/hedging behaviors for streaming and non-streaming calls. Provide example configs, migration guide, and tests for each language. Goal: reduce customer configuration surface while improving out-of-the-box reliability for mixed workloads (low-latency interactive vs high-throughput batch).
background: Customers repeatedly ask for simple guidance that works across languages. We currently surface fine-grained knobs that are powerful but confusing: pool sizes, idle timeouts, socket keep-alive, retry backoff, streaming re-establish semantics. Support tickets and SRE alerts show two recurring failure modes: (1) under-provisioned pools for bursty requests leading to high latency and queuing; (2) overly aggressive retries that amplify spikes for streaming responses. We need compact presets plus explicit streaming-safe retry semantics.
proposal:
- Define three named presets: conservative, balanced, aggressive. Each preset defines: max connections per host, per-connection concurrency, idle_reap_seconds, keepalive_probe_seconds, early_close_threshold, max_inflight_requests_per_connection, and retry strategy.
- Introduce per-route latency window hints (fast|medium|slow) that influence the preset selection and timeouts (deadline heuristics).
- For streaming RPCs: default to stream-first retry where a single client-initiated reconnect is allowed with transparent resume semantics when the model supports KV cache continuation; otherwise fall back to fail-fast with structured error explaining manual retry.
- Provide language examples and config APIs: Python: TransportPreset object; TS: TransportProfiles map; Go: TransportConfigurator builder.
acceptance_criteria: Three presets implemented and wired into Python/TS/Go SDKs with consistent semantics
Documentation page with examples for interactive low-latency and high-throughput batch use cases
Unit and integration tests validating pool sizing behavior and idle reclamation under synthetic burst workload
Streaming tests showing stream-first reconnect allowed once for compatible models, with clear fallbacks for non-compatible models
Migration guide and default behavior preserved for existing customers unless they opt-in to new presets
tradeoffs: Conservative preset reduces max concurrency and favors connection reuse — lower resource usage but can increase tail latency under bursts
Aggressive preset prioritizes throughput with higher connection count and shorter idle timeouts — higher cost and potential for TCP churn in client VPCs
Stream-first reconnect introduces complexity around resume tokens / KV cache compatibility; we limit automatic reconnects to a single attempt to bound nondeterminism
Per-route latency hints are heuristic and may not capture every workload; we provide overrides for advanced users
implementation_notes:
Key implementation points:
- Add a small TransportPreset registry in each SDK that maps preset -> concrete runtime settings. Keep the registry serializable to a single JSON file for diagnostics.
- Expose an opt-in legacy_compat flag to keep current defaults for customers who rely on present behavior.
- For streaming, wire in a StreamResume helper that consults the model capability map; if resume token present and model supports resume, attempt one reconnect using exponential backoff capped at 250ms; otherwise return structured StreamingNotResumable error.
- Instrument telemetry: preset_used, per_route_latency_hint, pool_reap_count, reconnect_attempts, retry_backoffs. Ensure we don't emit PII.
- Add e2e scenario that runs a simulated burst (1000 short requests over 5s) and validates 95th percentile latency stays within target for balanced preset.
code_examples:
Python example:
from redwood import TransportPreset, Client
# choose 'balanced' for general purpose
client = Client(transport_preset=TransportPreset.balanced(), per_route_hint={'/v1/chat': 'fast'})
# streaming: use resume token if provided
stream = client.chat_stream(prompt)
TypeScript example:
import { TransportProfiles, Client } from '@redwood/sdk'
const client = new Client({ transportProfile: TransportProfiles['balanced'], routeHints: { '/v1/generate': 'medium' } })
Go example:
cfg := sdk.NewTransportConfigurator().Preset(sdk.PresetBalanced).RouteHint("/v1/embed", "slow").Build()
cli := sdk.NewClient(cfg)
tests: Unit: preset -> expected numeric values for pool size and idle timeout across languages
Integration: synthetic burst workload for balanced and aggressive presets verifying p50/p95 latency targets
Streaming: simulated server that supports resume token; validate single reconnect resumes sequence without duplicate tokens
Chaos: simulate network partition and verify conservative preset doesn't trigger thundering herd retries
progress_updates: 2026-03-06: RFC written and reviewed by runtime and SDK leads (Aisha, Carlos, Mei). Decided on three named presets to keep UX simple.
2026-03-09: Python transport registry prototype implemented. Basic telemetry fields added to diagnostic event schema.
2026-03-11: Spike showed aggressive preset reduces client-side queuing but increases ephemeral connections in our test VPC — flagged as acceptable for aggressive with docs note.
2026-03-13: TS and Go teams started PRs for the profile map. Cross-language integration tests drafted.
2026-03-14: Design review with product and SRE. Product requested clearer migration messaging and a console toggle for enterprise customers to globally set default preset.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): land SDK changes behind feature flag for 10% of new SDK downloads and run e2e tests for 48h. Phase 2: enable preset registry by default in minor release and publish migration guide. Phase 3: add console control for enterprise tenants and backfill telemetry dashboards. Communicate with customers via release notes and migration docs.
notes_for_docs: Doc pages to include: 1) What each preset means in plain language and numeric defaults, 2) When to pick each preset (example workloads), 3) Per-route latency hints and examples, 4) Streaming behavior and how resume tokens work, 5) Troubleshooting guide with telemetry fields to inspect. Include sample JSON for TransportPreset and SDK-specific copy-paste examples.
follow_up_actions: Finalize numeric defaults and land RFC into sdk-* repos
Create dashboard queries for preset_used and pool_reap_count
